newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-FIFA ENTERS WORLD CUP ROW.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-FIFA ENTERS WORLD CUP ROW.

text.p: FIFA stepped into the row over the venue for the 2006 World Cup on Monday by saying it was perfectly acceptable for two nations from the same continent to bid.
And UEFA has confirmed it -- and English officials -- knew of Germany's interest as far back as June 1993.
The English F.A. which has not made an official bid, has been fuming after it emerged last week that UEFA is to back Germany's campaign.
But FIFA spokesman Keith Cooper said on Monday that UEFA's position would have no effect on the final decision.
"It is quite clear in the regulations that each and every one of the national associations is entitled to bid," he said on BBC radio.
"We have never had a continental confederation doing this on their (Germany's) behalf but the decision will be taken solely on the technical content of the bid."

However, FIFA will certainly want to avoid a situation similar to that of the 2002 World Cup which will now be shared between Japan and South Korea following the two Asian nations' long, expensive and often acrimonious bidding campaigns.

With the next tournament taking place in France, it is by no means a certainty that FIFA will want to return to Europe so soon. Africa is still awaiting its first World Cup and Latin America, which traditionally alternated with Europe, has not played host since 1986.
But that seemed far from the minds of those at the English F.A. on Monday who instead concentrated on arguing over the timing of the rival European bids.

The F.A.'s director of public affairs, David Davies, had said he was "incredulous" at UEFA's claim that English officials have known of the German bid for three years and chief executive Graham Kelly said he was still awaiting evidence from UEFA of when it agreed to back Germany.
Central to the disagreement appears to be former F.A. chairman Sir Bert Millichip, who denied any knowledge of an agreement between UEFA and Germany.

Millichip, an observer at UEFA's executive committee meeting in Lisbon last week, said on Monday: "I can confirm that no decision was ever minuted on supporting any specific country from Europe for the 2006 World Cup bid by the UEFA executive prior to last Wednesday."
UEFA general secretary Gerhard Aigner confirmed on Monday that although no decision was minuted, discussions about Germany's bid certainly were.
"We first talked about the subject on 24 June 1992 when the matter was discussed as part of trying to avoid two associations bidding for the same event," said Aigner.

"The following year, when discussing Vision One (FIFA's plan to alternate the hosting of the World Cup between continents), we talked about the fact that Germany was the first and only country to submit a bid for 2006.
"It was confirmed on 22nd June 1993 and Sir Bert (Millichip) was definitely present at those meetings."
Aigner added that he had sent a fax to Kelly asking to arrange a meeting for later this week.

FIFA vice-president, Scotland's David Will, said: "What happened is that two years ago UEFA decided it wanted a change to the FIFA rules, meaning that only one association in each continental confederation should make a World Cup bid.
"At that time Germany was the only country in Europe interested in 2006 and UEFA decided then it would totally support a German bid.
"Now England have joined the race but UEFA feels that having said that to Germany it is committed and has a problem in reversing that commitment."
The English F.A. decided to bid following the success of Euro 96 and was to announce its intention officially on February 12.
The deadline for bids is February 1999 and the decision will be made in June 2000.
